analogy.p: Imagine a crowd of people walking up a gentle hill: nobody stands at exactly the same height at any distance, but on average the further along the path they are, the higher they are. The scatter of people is the scatter graph, the path is the line of best fit, and a tight crowd on the path is strong correlation. It breaks down because the hill ends at the top, which is like extrapolating beyond the data, and because a real hill is a fixed path whereas a line of best fit is only an estimate drawn from the data.
analogy.t: A crowd walking up a hill

bullets: **Bivariate data** = two variables measured for each person or item, written as pairs (x, y).
Put the **independent variable** (the one that may influence the other, for example hours of revision) on the **x-axis** and the **dependent variable** (for example test score) on the y-axis.
Both axes need a **linear scale**, a label and units, and the scales must be chosen so the points fill most of the graph.
Plot each point carefully: along to the x-value, up to the y-value. Marks are lost for points more than half a small square out.
A scatter graph shows **relationships**, whereas a bar chart or pie chart shows how data is distributed.
You may be asked to **complete** a scatter graph by plotting extra points from a table, so practise reading scales.
core.p: A **scatter graph** is used to show the relationship between two sets of data, called **bivariate data**, where each item has two measurements (for example, hours of revision and test score for each student). Each pair of values is plotted as one point (usually a small cross or dot), with one variable on the x-axis and the other on the y-axis. The purpose is to see at a glance whether the two variables are linked and, if so, how. Scatter graphs are the Edexcel way of investigating whether a relationship exists before using it to make predictions.

bullets: **Positive correlation**: both variables increase together (for example, height and shoe size).
**Negative correlation**: as one variable increases the other decreases (for example, age of a car and its value).
**No correlation**: the points are scattered with no pattern (for example, shoe size and test score).
Describe it in the context of the question: 'As the number of hours revised increases, the test score tends to increase'.
Correlation describes the **trend**, not the exact value of any one point; there will always be some scatter.
The word 'relationship' or 'correlation' must be included in a written answer; just writing 'it goes up' will not earn the mark.
A **non-linear** pattern (for example a curve) is not described by these words: say there is a relationship but it is not linear, if it comes up.
core.p: **Correlation** describes the type of relationship between the two variables. If the points tend to go **up from left to right**, the variables have **positive correlation**: as one increases, the other increases. If the points go **down from left to right** there is **negative correlation**: as one increases, the other decreases. If the points show no pattern at all there is **no correlation**, which means there is no linear relationship between the variables.

bullets: **Strong correlation**: the points lie close to a straight line.
**Weak correlation**: the points are spread out around a general trend.
A perfect straight line of points is **perfect correlation**, which rarely appears in real data.
Predictions from a **strong** correlation are more reliable than from a weak one.
If you are asked to **describe** a scatter graph, give type and strength in context: 'strong negative correlation between age and value'.
Strength and type are independent: you can have a strong negative or a weak negative correlation.
core.p: Correlation can be **strong** or **weak**. The strength tells you how closely the points follow a straight line. If the points are all very close to a line you have **strong correlation**; if they are widely scattered but still show a general trend you have **weak correlation**. A stronger correlation means that predictions made from the line of best fit will be more reliable. Exam questions usually ask you to name the type and the strength together, for example 'strong positive correlation'.

bullets: Use a **ruler** and draw a single **straight** line; never join the dots or draw a curve.
The line should pass through the **middle** of the cloud, with about as many points above as below.
The line should **extend across the data** and, for estimates, may be extended slightly in both directions.
It does **not** need to go through the origin, and it does not have to touch any points.
A good method: find the mean of x and the mean of y and make the line pass through that point (mean point), then match the slope of the points.
If there is **no correlation**, a line of best fit is not appropriate.
Ignore clear **outliers** when drawing the line, but you can still show them on the plot.
core.h: Drawing a line of best fit
core.p: A **line of best fit** is a single straight line drawn through the middle of the points that shows the general trend of the data. It is drawn by eye using a ruler. It does not have to go through the origin or through any particular point, but it should have roughly the same number of points on each side of it and follow the trend of the data. The line is used to make estimates of one variable from the other. Marks are given for a line that is within the expected tolerance of the exact mean line, and for being straight and drawn with a ruler.

bullets: Step 1: find the given value on the axis (for example 4.5 hours on the x-axis).
Step 2: go up to the line of best fit and then across to the y-axis.
Step 3: read the value from the scale carefully, and write it with units: about 57%.
Using the equation y = 6x + 30: y = 6 × 4.5 + 30 = 27 + 30 = 57.
**Interpolation** = estimating **inside** the range of the data; usually **reliable**.
Draw your construction lines (dashed) on the graph because the examiner awards a mark for them.
The reliability is greater when the correlation is **strong** and when there are many data points.
core.h: Using the line of best fit: interpolation
core.p: The line of best fit lets us estimate a value of one variable given a value of the other. To do this, draw a line from the given value on one axis to the line of best fit, then across (or down) to the other axis and read off the estimate. Using the line to estimate within the range of the data is called **interpolation**, and it is generally reliable, especially when the correlation is strong. Always say the answer is an estimate and give units.

bullets: **Extrapolation** = estimating **outside** the range of the data. It is **unreliable**.
Reason to quote: **'the relationship may not continue outside the range of the data'**.
Example of an impossible prediction: 102% in a test marked out of 100.
Another example: predicting the height of a 40-year-old from a child growth graph.
A good answer names the specific reason in context rather than just writing 'it is unreliable'.
Interpolation is reliable, extrapolation is not: **learn both words and which is which**.
Extending the line only slightly beyond the data is less risky than extending far beyond it, but still carries a risk.
core.h: Extrapolation and why it is unreliable
core.p: Using the line of best fit to estimate values **outside the range of the data** is called **extrapolation**. This is unreliable because we do not know that the same relationship continues beyond the data we collected. A trend that was straight within the data may curve, level off, or stop completely. In the revision example, extending the line to 12 hours predicts a score of 6 × 12 + 30 = 102%, which is impossible because the maximum score is 100%. That is a clear exam example of why extrapolation cannot be trusted.

bullets: **Gradient = change in y ÷ change in x** (rise ÷ run). Choose two points on the line that are far apart for accuracy.
Interpretation: **'for each extra hour of revision the test score increases by 6 marks, on average'**.
**y-intercept**: where the line crosses the y-axis; interpretation: predicted y when x = 0, but check if x = 0 makes sense.
A **negative gradient** matches negative correlation: y decreases as x increases.
Use the line equation to check readings: at x = 6, y = 6 × 6 + 30 = 66, which matches the graph.
This links to the straight line graphs topic: y = mx + c and finding the equation of a line.
core.h: Meaning of the gradient and the intercept
core.p: The line of best fit is a straight line, so it has an equation of the form y = mx + c. The **gradient** m tells you how much y changes for each 1 unit increase in x, and the **y-intercept** c is the value of y when x = 0. In context, this lets you explain what the line says about the real situation. In our revision example y = 6x + 30, the gradient 6 means that on average each extra hour of revision is linked with 6 more marks, and the intercept 30 is the predicted score with no revision.

bullets: An outlier is a point **well away from the rest** of the pattern.
**Ignore outliers** when drawing the line of best fit.
Possible reasons: a **recording error**, a typing mistake, or an unusual individual.
If asked to **circle** an outlier, circle the single point that is far from the trend.
Do not remove data without a reason; mention it and state that the correlation description is for the remaining points.
A single outlier can make a correlation look weaker than it really is.
core.p: An **outlier** is a data point that does not fit the general pattern of the other points; it lies a long way from the trend. Outliers can be caused by mistakes in recording or measuring, or by unusual cases that are genuinely different. When drawing a line of best fit you should **ignore outliers** because they would pull the line away from the trend of the rest of the data. In a written answer, you can point out the outlier and suggest a possible reason.

bullets: **Correlation ≠ causation**: a link between two variables does not prove one causes the other.
A **third variable** (hot weather in the example) can cause both changes.
A link can be a **coincidence**, particularly in small data sets.
Model phrase: **'There is correlation but this does not prove that one causes the other.'**
To argue for causation you need more evidence, such as a controlled experiment or a known mechanism.
If a question asks 'Does this show that X causes Y?', the answer is almost always **no**, with a reason.
core.p: Correlation shows that two variables **change together**, but it does not prove that one **causes** the other. There may be a third variable (a lurking variable) causing both, or the link may be a coincidence. For example, ice cream sales and sunburn cases are positively correlated, but ice cream does not cause sunburn: hot weather increases both. Edexcel examiners reward answers that say there is a correlation but cannot conclude that one causes the other without further evidence.

bullets: Work out the value of **one small square** on each axis before reading or plotting.
Plot points with a **sharp pencil** as small crosses, within half a small square.
Draw lines of best fit with a **ruler**, not freehand.
Show **construction lines** when reading an estimate from the graph.
If the axis does not start at zero, there may be a **break** in the axis; read the scale carefully.
State the answer with **units** and the word **estimate**, for example 'about 57%'.
Check the answer makes sense in context (a test score cannot be above 100%).
core.h: Reading scatter graphs: accuracy and good practice
core.p: Examiners give marks for accurate plotting, for using a ruler, and for clear reading. Take the time to choose a sensible scale if the axes are not given and always label them. When reading values from the graph, work out what each small square represents before you read off. Write units with every estimate. These simple habits protect the marks that are easiest to earn.

bullets: Compare the **type** (positive, negative, none) and **strength** (strong, weak) for each graph.
The graph with points **closer to its line** has stronger correlation, so predictions are more reliable.
Link: **y = mx + c** and gradient from the straight line graphs topic.
Link: mean of x and mean of y give the **mean point** that the line of best fit passes through (from averages).
Link: **time series** and **cumulative frequency** graphs are other statistical diagrams, but only scatter graphs show correlation between two variables.
Scatter graph questions appear on all three papers and are typically **2 to 4 marks**.
core.p: You may be asked to compare two scatter graphs, or to decide which of two variables gives the better prediction. Compare the **type** and **strength** of the correlation: the graph with points closer to the line has the stronger correlation and gives more reliable predictions. Scatter graphs link to several other topics: the equation of the line of best fit links to straight line graphs, and the mean point links to averages from the statistics topics.

bullets: **Describe**: type (positive, negative, none) + strength (strong, weak) + the two variables named in context.
**Compare**: the graph whose points lie **closer to the line** has the stronger correlation and gives the more reliable estimates.
**Do not write** that the graph shows what causes what; write about the relationship or correlation only.
**Complete a graph**: use the table, work out the scale of one small square, plot each pair (x, y) as a small cross.
**Mean point**: (mean of x, mean of y) always lies on the best-fit line; for the example it is (4.5, 57.5).
**Reliable estimate** = interpolation + strong correlation + many data points.
**Unreliable estimate** = extrapolation, or weak correlation, or very few points.
core.h: Describing and comparing scatter graphs: model answers
core.p: Examiners reward answers that name the type, the strength and the context together, and that use the word correlation. A full description of the revision example is: there is strong positive correlation between hours of revision and test score, so as revision time increases, the score tends to increase. To compare two graphs, state which has the stronger correlation by saying which has points closer to its line of best fit, then say which will give the more reliable predictions. You should also be ready to give a reason when a prediction is not reliable.

exam: **Describe the correlation** (usually 1 mark): write 'positive' or 'negative' (with 'strong' or 'weak' if asked) and say 'correlation'. For the context mark write 'as hours of revision increase, test score increases'.
**Draw a line of best fit** (1 or 2 marks): a straight ruled line that follows the trend with roughly equal points either side; it is accepted within a tolerance.
**Use your line to estimate** (2 marks): 1 mark for a valid construction on the graph or a reading from your line, 1 mark for the value within tolerance. Show dashed lines.

**'Comment on the reliability'** of an estimate: if it is within the data say it is **reliable (interpolation)** and the correlation is strong; if outside say **unreliable (extrapolation)** as the trend may not continue.
**'Does this show that X causes Y?'** Answer 'No' and give the reason: correlation does not mean causation, another factor may cause both.
**Plot the points**: marks for points within half a small square; use a sharp pencil.
**Interpret the gradient** (2 marks): 'for each extra 1 unit of x, y increases by (gradient) units, on average'. Always include the units.
**Circle the outlier**: circle the one point clearly away from the pattern; do not circle several.
**Write the type of correlation for a given sketch** by checking if points go up (positive), down (negative) or random (none).
Scatter graph questions appear on **all three papers**; Paper 1 is non-calculator so the line equation will have friendly numbers.
Quote **exact words** in written answers: correlation, interpolation, extrapolation, outlier, causation.

mistakes.r: Draw one straight line with a ruler through the middle of the points.
mistakes.w: Joining the points with a zigzag line or drawing a curve for the line of best fit.

mistakes.r: Write 'positive correlation' and describe it in context: as x increases, y tends to increase.
mistakes.w: Writing 'the graph goes up' as the description.

mistakes.r: Extrapolation is outside the range of the data and is unreliable because the trend may not continue.
mistakes.w: Saying extrapolation is reliable if the correlation is strong.

mistakes.r: Correlation does not prove causation; there may be another factor or coincidence.
mistakes.w: Writing that the correlation proves one variable causes the other.

mistakes.r: The line need not pass through (0, 0); follow the trend of the points.
mistakes.w: Forcing the line of best fit through the origin.

mistakes.r: Ignore outliers when drawing the line of best fit.
mistakes.w: Letting an outlier drag the line of best fit.

mistakes.r: Draw lines from the axis to the line and across, read carefully and give units.
mistakes.w: Reading a value from the graph without showing construction lines or without units.

mistakes.r: Strength depends on how close the points are to the line, not on the gradient.
mistakes.w: Describing the strength by how steep the line is.

mistakes.r: Correlation shows variables change together; cause needs more evidence, such as a controlled experiment.
mistakes.w: Writing that a strong correlation proves one variable causes the other.

mistakes.r: Draw one straight line with a ruler through the middle of the points.
mistakes.w: Joining the points to make a zigzag or a curve for the line of best fit.

summary: You need to plot and interpret scatter graphs, describe the type and strength of correlation, draw and use a line of best fit to estimate values, and distinguish interpolation from extrapolation. You must also recognise outliers and explain that correlation does not prove causation. Key skills: describe type and strength in context, draw a ruler line through the mean point, use it to interpolate, explain why extrapolation is unreliable, read the gradient and intercept of y = mx + c, spot outliers, and state that correlation does not prove causation.

terms.d: A graph that plots pairs of values as points to show whether there is a relationship between two variables.
Data with two variables recorded for each item, written as pairs (x, y).
A measure of the type and strength of the relationship between two variables.
As one variable increases, the other variable also increases.
As one variable increases, the other variable decreases.
There is no relationship between the two variables; the points show no pattern.
The points lie close to a straight line.
The points are widely scattered about the trend.
A straight line drawn through the middle of the points on a scatter graph that shows the general trend.
Estimating a value within the range of the data using the line of best fit; generally reliable.
Estimating a value outside the range of the data using the line of best fit; unreliable.
A data point that does not fit the general pattern of the rest of the data.
One variable directly causes a change in the other.
The variable that is changed or thought to influence the other; plotted on the x-axis.
The variable that responds to the other; plotted on the y-axis.
The change in y divided by the change in x along a straight line.
The point (mean of x, mean of y); a line of best fit should pass through or very close to it.
A third variable that affects both measured variables and can create correlation without cause.
The span of x-values actually collected; estimates inside it are interpolation, outside it are extrapolation.
